word_order: SVO | Subjects precede verbs and objects follow verbs in the samples (e.g. "Travellers are strongly advised...", "He has been unable to take the drugs...")
punctuation_present: always — as observed in the sample
register: edited written prose / informational (encyclopedic, travel, news-like) text
target_language_risks: Pronoun and case ambiguity: fragments can leave antecedents unresolved (he/it/they, whom/who), causing wrong gender/case in German.
Verb placement/split verbs: German subordinate clauses and separable verbs require verb-final or particle placement that may depend on later material; early splitting can force incorrect ordering.
Auxiliary/modal dependencies and tense/aspect: auxiliaries (has/have/will/can) need their complements to render correct German tense or modality.
Attachment ambiguity: prepositional phrases or relative clauses may attach to different nouns; translating a fragment can fix a wrong attachment.
Unbalanced punctuation/quotes/parentheses and abbreviations (e.g., Dr.) can break sentence reconstruction if split incorrectly.
notes_for_prompt_writer: Do not place <SEG> immediately before trailing punctuation (commas, semicolons, closing quotes/parentheses) or at abbreviations containing periods (Dr., etc.). Keep subordinating conjunctions and their clause material together (if/when/after/since/that/which/who). Avoid splitting between auxiliaries/modals and their complements or between subjects and their main verbs; prefer splits at full sentences or after strong clause-closing punctuation.
